Please describe your king mackerel obser:
As a U.S. Navy veteran and full-time charter captain operating out of Surfside Beach, Texas, I’ve spent more than a decade on the Gulf of America. Over that time, I’ve watched the king mackerel fishery change dramatically—and not for the better.

Years ago, kingfish were a dependable part of nearly every offshore trip. It wasn’t uncommon to catch multiple fish in a day, and fish weighing 40 to 50 pounds were realistic targets. During tournaments, those weights were expected to be competitive.

Today, the fishery tells a much different story.

Over roughly the last five years, kingfish numbers have noticeably declined off the upper Texas coast. Many trips that once produced consistent action now result in only one or two fish—or none at all. It’s become common for an entire charter to celebrate catching just a single kingfish. Tournament-winning fish have also become significantly smaller, with many events now being won by fish in the upper-30-pound range rather than the 50-pound class fish that were once regularly seen.

This decline isn’t something I’ve observed alone. It’s a consistent topic of conversation among charter captains, recreational anglers, and tournament fishermen throughout our area. Many of us have noticed the same trend despite improvements in electronics, boats, and fishing techniques.

While there are likely multiple contributing factors—including environmental changes, forage availability, habitat conditions, and fishing pressure—the overall reduction in abundance appears significant enough to warrant additional scientific evaluation. Better understanding spawning success, recruitment, migration patterns, and regional stock distribution could help explain what many of us are seeing firsthand on the water.

As someone who fishes nearly every suitable weather day during the season, my perspective is based on thousands of hours offshore rather than isolated experiences. The king mackerel fishery has historically been an important recreational and economic resource for the Texas coast, supporting charter businesses, tournaments, tourism, and countless family traditions.

I hope continued collaboration between anglers, charter captains, fisheries managers, and researchers will help identify the causes behind this apparent decline so future generations can experience the same exciting kingfish fishery many of us were fortunate enough to enjoy.

Please describe your king mackerel obser: Kings have been in decline in the western gulf, my port is Galveston, TX since about 2022. We started having a harder time catching 2 per person (we never went to 3 per person) and by 2024 we were having a hard time just finding a few for the boat and in 2025, (we run 2 permitted boats), we only caught 8 between both boats for the entire summer and so far this year have not seen a king at all. Nor have I heard of any being caught all the way up the coast. We lost over 200 near shore platforms in the last 10 years and I know that hurt us some, but kings didn’t stop migrating because of that. My theory is the new recruits got killed off by red tide or some other algae bloom and/or sharks and dolphins probably ate a few but I believe it has more to do with sea temps and low oxygen. Because kings sink when they die instead of float it’s hard to know exactly what happened. But whatever happened it’s a problem I wish we could figure out and get fixed.

Please describe your king mackerel obser: Something seems to have changed over the last 5 years out of Texas. You used to be able to catch all the kingfish you wanted at any rig from 5-30 miles out. It seems the kingfish have disappeared anywhere past 10 miles offshore. We are still finding them in concentrated pockets over natural hard bottom in 50-70 feet of water. However, the numbers overall seem down and they are not as widespread. We fish an annual tournament out of surfside Texas every year since 2019. The first few years, the winning kingfish were over 50 pounds. The winning size has decreased every year. Last year not a single fish over 30 pounds was caught. Also, The annual Fishing Fiesta in Freeport Texas was held 4th of July weekend. This is a 3 day tournament that occurred during great weather this year. The winning fish was only 19 pounds. Something needs to be done about our kingfish stock. They are a great angling opportunity for smaller boats that can’t run far offshore.
